6.0.oldText: SOCRATES: I have heard a tradition of the ancients — whether true or not, only they know. But if we had found the truth ourselves, do you think we would care much about the opinions of men?

6.1.oldText: PHAEDRUS: Your question needs no answer — but I wish you'd tell me what you say you have heard.

6.2.oldText: SOCRATES: At the Egyptian city of Naucratis, there was a famous old god whose name was Theuth. The bird called the Ibis is sacred to him, and he was the inventor of many arts — arithmetic and calculation and geometry and astronomy and draughts and dice — but his great discovery was the use of letters. Now in those days the god Thamus was the king of the whole country of Egypt; he dwelt in that great city of Upper Egypt which the Greeks call Egyptian Thebes, and the god himself is called by them Ammon. To him came Theuth and showed his inventions, asking that the other Egyptians might be allowed to have the benefit of them. He enumerated them, and Thamus inquired about their several uses, and praised some and censured others according as he approved or disapproved. It would take a long time to repeat all that Thamus said to Theuth in praise or blame of the various arts. But when they came to letters, 'This,' said Theuth, 'will make the Egyptians wiser and give them better memories — it is a specific both for memory and for wit.' Thamus replied: 'O most ingenious Theuth, the parent or inventor of an art is not always the best judge of the usefulness or uselessness of his own inventions to the users of them. In this instance, you, the father of letters, from a paternal love of your own children, have been led to attribute to them a quality they cannot have. For this discovery of yours will create forgetfulness in the learners' souls, because they will not use their memories — they will trust to external written characters and not remember of themselves. The specific you have discovered is an aid not to memory, but to reminiscence; and you give your disciples not truth, but only the semblance of truth. They will be hearers of many things and will have learned nothing. They will appear to be omniscient and will generally know nothing. They will be tiresome company, having the show of wisdom without the reality.'

6.4.oldText: SOCRATES: There was a tradition in the temple of Dodona that oaks first gave prophetic utterances. The men of old, unlike young philosophy in their simplicity, thought that if they heard the truth even from 'oak or rock,' that was enough for them — whereas you seem to consider not whether a thing is or is not true, but who the speaker is and from what country the tale comes.

6.5.oldText: PHAEDRUS: I acknowledge the justice of your rebuke. And I think the Theban is right in his view about letters.

6.6.oldText: SOCRATES: He would be a very simple person, and quite a stranger to the oracles of Thamus or Ammon, who would leave any art in writing or receive it in writing under the idea that the written word would be intelligible or certain — or who supposed that writing was in any way better than knowledge and recollection of the same matters.

6.8.oldText: SOCRATES: I can't help feeling, Phaedrus, that writing is unfortunately like painting. The creations of the painter have the attitude of life — yet if you ask them a question, they preserve a solemn silence. The same may be said of speeches. You would imagine they had intelligence; but if you want to know something and put a question to one of them, the speaker always gives one unvarying answer. And when they have once been written down, they are tumbled about anywhere among those who may or may not understand them. They do not know whom they should reply to and whom not. And if they are maltreated or abused, they have no parent to protect them — they cannot protect or defend themselves.

6.9.oldText: PHAEDRUS: That again is most true.

6.10.oldText: SOCRATES: Is there not another kind of word or speech far better than this, and having far greater power — a son of the same family, but lawfully begotten?

6.11.oldText: PHAEDRUS: Whom do you mean, and what is his origin?

6.12.oldText: SOCRATES: I mean an intelligent word graven in the soul of the learner, which can defend itself, and knows when to speak and when to be silent.

6.13.oldText: PHAEDRUS: You mean the living word of knowledge which has a soul, and of which the written word is properly no more than an image?

6.14.oldText: SOCRATES: Yes, that's exactly what I mean. And now may I be allowed to ask you a question: would a farmer who is a man of sense take the seeds he values and which he wants to bear fruit, and in sober seriousness plant them during the heat of summer in some garden of Adonis, so that he can rejoice when he sees them appearing in beauty in eight days? He would only do that, if at all, for amusement and pastime. But when he's in earnest, he sows in fitting soil, and practices husbandry, and is satisfied if in eight months the seeds he has sown come to perfection?

6.15.oldText: PHAEDRUS: Yes, Socrates, that will be his way when he's in earnest; he'll do the other, as you say, only in play.

6.16.oldText: SOCRATES: And can we suppose that he who knows the just and good and honorable has less understanding about his own seeds than the farmer about his?

6.18.oldText: SOCRATES: Then he will not seriously incline to 'write' his thoughts 'in water' with pen and ink, sowing words which can neither speak for themselves nor teach the truth adequately to others?

6.20.oldText: SOCRATES: No, that's not likely. In the garden of letters he will sow and plant, but only for recreation and amusement. He will write his thoughts down as memorials, to be treasured against the forgetfulness of old age, by himself or by any other old man treading the same path. He'll rejoice in beholding their tender growth; and while others are refreshing their souls with banqueting and the like, this will be the pastime in which his days are spent.

6.21.oldText: PHAEDRUS: A pastime, Socrates, as noble as the other is ignoble — the pastime of a man who can be amused by serious talk, and can discourse merrily about justice and the like.

6.22.oldText: SOCRATES: True, Phaedrus. But far nobler is the serious pursuit of the dialectician, who, finding a congenial soul, by the help of science sows and plants in it words that are able to help themselves and the man who planted them, and are not unfruitful, but have in them a seed which others, brought up in different soils, render immortal — making those who possess it happy to the utmost extent of human happiness.

6.24.oldText: SOCRATES: And now, Phaedrus, having agreed on the premises, we may decide about the conclusion.

6.26.oldText: SOCRATES: About Lysias, whom we censured, and his art of writing, and his speeches, and the rhetorical skill or want of skill shown in them. These were the questions we sought to determine, and they brought us to this point. And I think we are now pretty well informed about the nature of art and its opposite.

6.27.oldText: PHAEDRUS: Yes, I think so too — but I wish you'd repeat what was said.

6.28.oldText: SOCRATES: Until a man knows the truth of the several particulars he is writing or speaking about, and is able to define them as they are, and having defined them is able to divide them again until they can no longer be divided; and until in the same way he is able to discern the nature of the soul, and discover the different modes of discourse adapted to different natures, and arrange and dispose them in such a way that the simple form of speech is addressed to the simpler nature, and the complex and composite to the more complex nature — until he has accomplished all this, he will be unable to handle arguments according to rules of art, as far as their nature allows them to be subjected to art, either for teaching or for persuading. Such is the view implied by the whole preceding argument.

6.29.oldText: PHAEDRUS: Yes, that was our view, certainly.

6.30.oldText: SOCRATES: Secondly, as to the censure passed on the speaking or writing of discourses, and how they might be rightly or wrongly censured — didn't our previous argument show?

6.32.oldText: SOCRATES: That whether it's Lysias or any other writer who ever was or will be, whether private man or statesman, who proposes laws and so becomes the author of a political treatise, fancying that there is great certainty and clarity in his performance — the fact of his writing it is only a disgrace to him, whatever men may say. For not to know the nature of justice and injustice, and good and evil, and not to be able to distinguish the dream from the reality, cannot in truth be otherwise than disgraceful to him, even if he has the applause of the whole world.

6.34.oldText: SOCRATES: But he who thinks that in the written word there is necessarily much that is not serious — and that neither poetry nor prose, spoken or written, is of any great value if, like the compositions of the rhapsodes, they are only recited to be believed and not with any view to criticism or instruction; and who thinks that even the best of writings are only a reminiscence of what we know, and that only in principles of justice and goodness and nobility taught and communicated orally for the sake of instruction and graven in the soul (which is the true way of writing) is there clarity and perfection and seriousness; and that such principles are a man's own and his legitimate offspring — first, the word he finds in his own bosom, and secondly, the brethren and descendants and relations of his idea which have been duly implanted by him in the souls of others; and who cares for these and no others — this is the right sort of man, and you and I, Phaedrus, would pray that we may become like him.

6.35.oldText: PHAEDRUS: That is most assuredly my desire and prayer.

6.36.oldText: SOCRATES: And now the play is played out, and of rhetoric enough. Go and tell Lysias that to the fountain and school of the Nymphs we went down, and were bidden by them to convey a message to him and to other composers of speeches — to Homer and other writers of poems, whether set to music or not; and to Solon and others who have composed writings in the form of political discourses which they would term laws. To all of them we are to say that if their compositions are based on knowledge of the truth, and they can defend or prove them, when put to the test, by spoken arguments that leave their writings poor by comparison — then they are to be called not only poets, orators, and legislators, but are worthy of a higher name, befitting the serious pursuit of their life.

6.37.oldText: PHAEDRUS: What name would you assign to them?

6.38.oldText: SOCRATES: Wise, I may not call them — for that is a great name which belongs to God alone. Lovers of wisdom, or philosophers, is their modest and befitting title.

6.40.oldText: SOCRATES: And he who cannot rise above his own compilations and compositions, which he has been long patching and piecing, adding some and taking away some, may be justly called poet or speech-maker or law-maker.

6.43.oldText: PHAEDRUS: But there is also a friend of yours who ought not to be forgotten.

6.45.oldText: PHAEDRUS: Isocrates the fair — what message will you send to him, and how shall we describe him?

6.46.oldText: SOCRATES: Isocrates is still young, Phaedrus; but I'm willing to hazard a prophecy concerning him.

6.48.oldText: SOCRATES: I think he has a genius that soars above the orations of Lysias, and that his character is cast in a finer mold. My impression is that he will marvelously improve as he grows older, and that all former rhetoricians will be as children in comparison. And I believe he will not be satisfied with rhetoric, but that there is in him a divine inspiration which will lead him to things higher still — for he has an element of philosophy in his nature. This is the message of the gods dwelling in this place, which I will myself deliver to Isocrates, who is my delight. And you give the other to Lysias, who is yours.

6.49.oldText: PHAEDRUS: I will. And now that the heat has abated, let us depart.

6.50.oldText: SOCRATES: Should we not first offer up a prayer to the local deities?

6.52.oldText: SOCRATES: Beloved Pan, and all you other gods who haunt this place, give me beauty in the inward soul; and may the outward and inward man be at one. May I reckon the wise to be the wealthy, and may I have such a quantity of gold as a temperate man, and he only, can bear and carry. Anything more? The prayer, I think, is enough for me.
